claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin iron oxide layer that may contain defects.
The native iron oxide layer on Q235 steel is sufficiently protective under room-temperature ambient conditions.
At 700–900 °C in an aggressive salt environment, the native oxide on Q235 becomes thermodynamically unstable.
The unstable Q235 oxide transforms into a porous scale or dissolves in the high-temperature salt.
Breakdown of the oxide permits salt species to penetrate to the underlying Q235 steel.
Salt penetration accelerates localized corrosion of the underlying Q235 steel.
The integrity and phase composition of the native iron oxide govern its barrier properties against salt penetration.
Compact magnetite is more protective than porous or dissolving oxide phases in this system.
Slow room-temperature oxidation forms a relatively compact and adherent oxide film that retards further Q235 corrosion.
Ion-exchange reactions and metal dissolution can contribute to corrosion in aggressive molten salts.
Q235 will exhibit minimal mass loss and retain a relatively intact oxide layer during room-temperature ambient exposure.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce greater mass loss, pitting, and a more porous or non-protective oxide scale on Q235 than room-temperature ambient exposure.
A well-alloyed stainless steel provides an appropriate reference having a more stable passivating oxide under the proposed high-temperature salt conditions.
Additional surface treatments or alloying elements can stabilize an oxide film and make the proposed native-oxide mechanism inapplicable.
Salt composition and impurity levels can change molten-salt corrosion reaction pathways.
Moisture in fluoride salt can form hydrofluoric acid that causes elemental dissolution from structural alloys.
